title: Acoustic Measures of Prosody in Individuals with Autism Spectrum Disorder
abstract:
Saadia Elahi

Faculty Advisor: Molly Losh, Ph.D.
Doctoral Student Mentor: Shivani Patel, M.A.

Acoustic Measures of Prosody in Individuals with Autism Spectrum Disorder

Difficulties in social communication are characteristic of individuals with autism spectrum disorder (ASD). These difficulties include atypical prosody, or the stress and intonation patterns of speech that are often critical to conveying emotion and intention. Prior work has noted variable prosodic profiles in ASD, such as sounding too monotone or too singsongy, based on listener ratings. To provide objective characterization of prosody in ASD, we assessed acoustic measures of pitch during affect expression (like vs. dislike) and turn-end type expression (statement vs. question production), both of which may negatively impact social interaction if used inappropriately. This study utilized speech samples from the Profiling Elements of Prosody in Speech-Communication (PEPS-C), a task assessing one’s ability to comprehend and produce prosody. Speech analysis software (Praat) was utilized to extract measures of mean, range, and standard deviation of fundamental frequency (F0) in a sample of 14 individuals with ASD and 11 typically developing (TD) controls. Linear mixed effects models, covarying for age and gender, were conducted to assess differences between ASD and TD groups. While no significant group differences emerged on the Turn-End subtest, results revealed significantly lower range of F0 on the Affect subtest in the ASD group, reflecting reduced pitch variability when conveying emotion. As such, reduced pitch variability during affect expression may be an important aspect of atypical prosody contributing to social communication deficits noted in ASD. Future work may seek to assess the utility of targeting pitch modulation to improve affect expression among individuals with ASD.
